title: Generics and utility types
summary: Generic functions and how TypeScript infers them, constraints with `extends keyof`, indexed access `T[K]`, default type parameters, typed data structures, the built-in utility types, `satisfies` versus annotation, and the mistakes that leak `any`.
prerequisiteNotes: ts-types-basics: structural typing, unions, literal types, narrowing and `unknown` versus `any`. Generics are functions over those types, so you need to read a union and a literal type fluently first.
objectives: Write generic functions whose type parameters are inferred from arguments, and say where each type parameter is inferred from.
Constrain a type parameter with `extends` and use `K extends keyof T` with `T[K]` to type property access precisely.
Build a generic data structure (stack, cache) with a class type parameter and a sensible default.
Choose the right built-in utility type: `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`, `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `NonNullable`, `Awaited`.
Explain when `satisfies` beats a type annotation, and why `as T` and `any` hide bugs because types are erased at runtime.
Spot an unnecessary type parameter and replace it with a plain parameter type.

concepts.title: Generic functions and inference
concepts.body: A type parameter is a placeholder the caller fills in. You almost never write it explicitly: TypeScript **infers** it from the arguments at each call site, so `first([1, 2])` gives `T = number` and `first(['a'])` gives `T = string`. The point of a generic is to **relate** types: the return type depends on the argument type. Without the type parameter you would choose between `unknown` (safe but useless to the caller) and `any` (useful but unchecked). When inference has nothing to work from, for example `new Map()` or `useState(null)`-style calls, it falls back to the constraint or `unknown`, and that is when you pass the type explicitly: `new Map<string, number>()`. A `const` type parameter (`<const T>`, TS 5.0) asks for literal inference, so `['a', 'b']` becomes `readonly ['a', 'b']` instead of `string[]`.

concepts.title: Constraints: extends, keyof and T[K]
concepts.body: `<T extends Shape>` means "any type, as long as it is assignable to `Shape`", which lets the body use `Shape`'s members while the caller keeps their more specific type. `keyof T` is the union of `T`'s property names, and `T[K]` (an **indexed access type**) is the type of property `K`. Together, `<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` rejects typos at compile time and returns the exact property type, `number` for `'age'` and `string` for `'name'`. Because `K` is inferred from a string literal it stays the literal `'age'`, not `string`. Note that `keyof` of a type with a string index signature is `string | number`, because numeric keys are converted to strings.

concepts.title: Default type parameters and generic data structures
concepts.body: Classes and interfaces take type parameters too: `class Stack<T>` stores `T[]` and every method shares that `T`, so pushing a string onto a `Stack<number>` is a compile error. A **default** (`<T = string>`) is used when the caller writes the type name without arguments or when inference finds nothing; it is not a constraint, and a default must satisfy any constraint on the same parameter. Parameters with defaults must come after required ones, like function parameters. For keyed structures prefer `Map<K, V>` over a plain object: a `Map` keeps the key's real type (`1` and `'1'` are different keys) and iterates in insertion order, while object keys are always strings.

concepts.title: Utility types that reshape an object type
concepts.body: The built-ins derive new types from one source of truth so they cannot drift. `Partial<T>` makes every property optional (patch payloads); `Required<T>` removes the `?`s; `Readonly<T>` marks properties `readonly` (compile time only, and shallow). `Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'>` keeps listed keys; `Omit<T, 'pw'>` removes them; `Record<K, V>` builds an object type with keys `K` and values `V`, and with a literal union for `K` it forces you to handle every key. Two traps: `Omit`'s key parameter is not checked against `T`, so `Omit<User, 'pasword'>` silently removes nothing; and none of these exist at runtime, so `Omit` never strips a property from an actual object. Under the hood they are **mapped types** (`{ [P in K]: T[P] }`), which you will author in a later advanced lesson.

concepts.title: Deriving types from values: ReturnType, Parameters, NonNullable, Awaited
concepts.body: Often the value is the source of truth and the type should follow it. `typeof fn` turns a value into its type; `ReturnType<typeof fn>` and `Parameters<typeof fn>` (a tuple) then extract the pieces, which is handy for wrapping a third-party function without re-declaring its types. `NonNullable<T>` removes `null` and `undefined` from a union. `Awaited<T>` unwraps promises recursively, so `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>>` is the resolved value of an async function. Reach for these when you would otherwise copy a type by hand; do not use them to obscure a type a reader needs to see.

concepts.title: satisfies versus a type annotation
concepts.body: An annotation `const x: T = value` **replaces** the inferred type with `T`: the value is checked, then forgotten. `const x = value satisfies T` (TS 4.9) **checks** the value against `T` but keeps the precise inferred type. Use an annotation when you want the wider type (a variable you will reassign, a public API boundary). Use `satisfies` for config tables and lookup maps: you still get excess-key and missing-key errors, but literal keys stay known, so a typo such as `routes.hmoe` is a compile error and each value keeps its own type. Combine it with `as const` (`{...} as const satisfies T`) to keep literal values as well.

concepts.title: Types are erased: as T and any leaks
concepts.body: Generics, annotations, `as` assertions and utility types are **deleted** when TypeScript emits JavaScript. A function such as `parse<T>(s): T { return JSON.parse(s) as T }` therefore promises whatever the caller asks for and checks nothing: `parse<number>('"42"')` returns a string typed as `number`. `JSON.parse`, `Response.json()` and `catch (e)` with loose settings give `any`, and `any` spreads: every property and call on it is also `any`, so errors surface far from the cause. Defend the boundary instead: type it as `unknown`, then narrow with a check or a type guard that runs at runtime, and only then hand out the precise type.

task: Write `groupBy(items, key)`. `items` is an array of objects and `key` is the name of one of their properties. Return the groups as an array of `[keyValue, itemsWithThatValue]` pairs, ordered by the **first appearance** of each key value, with items in their original order. Key values keep their real type: `1` and `'1'` are different groups, and a numeric key comes back as a number, not a string. Type it so the key must be a property of the items and the returned key values have that property's type (`Array<[T[K], T[]]>`).
hints: A plain object turns every key into a string and lists integer-like keys first in ascending order. Which built-in keeps the key's type and insertion order?
Use `new Map<T[K], T[]>()`, push each item into `map.get(item[key])` (creating the array on first sight), then return `[...map]`, which is already an array of `[key, group]` pairs.
checklist: The key parameter is `K extends keyof T`, so a misspelt property name is a compile error.
Group keys keep their type: numbers stay numbers and `1` is separate from `'1'`.
Groups appear in order of first appearance, including negative and integer-like keys.
An empty input returns `[]` and no `as` or `any` appears in my solution.
pitfalls: Adding a type parameter that is used only once, as in `function len<T extends string>(s: T): number`; write `s: string` instead.
Typing a key as `string` and indexing with `obj[key] as any`, which accepts typos and returns `any` instead of `T[K]`.
Expecting `Omit` or `Readonly` to change the object at runtime; types are erased, so the password is still there and the property is still writable.
Misspelling a key in `Omit<User, 'pasword'>`, which compiles because `Omit` does not check its keys against `T`.
Annotating a lookup table with a wide `Record<string, V>` and losing its literal keys, when `satisfies` would keep them.
Writing `JSON.parse(text) as T` and trusting it; validate `unknown` at the boundary instead.
Grouping into a plain object and getting string keys back in a different order from the input.

walkthrough.title: How a call site fills in T and K
walkthrough.body: Read a generic call the way the compiler does. For `pluck(users, 'age')` with signature `<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][]`, the first argument matches `T[]`, so `T = User`. The second argument is a string literal, so `K = 'age'`. The compiler then checks the constraint `'age'` against `keyof User`, and finally substitutes into the return type: `User['age'][]`, which is `number[]`. If you can narrate those four steps in an interview, you can debug almost any inference error message.

walkthrough.title: When a type parameter is not needed
walkthrough.body: A type parameter earns its place by appearing **at least twice**: in two parameters, or in a parameter and the return type, so it links them. `function show<T>(x: T): void` links nothing and is just `x: unknown`. `function size<T extends unknown[]>(xs: T): number` is just `xs: readonly unknown[]`. Extra type parameters make signatures harder to read and can make inference worse. The reverse mistake is returning `any` or `unknown` from something that should be generic, which forces every caller to cast. Ask: does the output type depend on the input type? If yes, generic; if no, plain types.

walkthrough.title: Solve the task in three moves
walkthrough.body: First, write the signature, because it is the interesting part: `<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): Array<[T[K], T[]]>`. Say why each piece is there. Second, pick the container: a `Map<T[K], T[]>` because keys keep their type and order; an object would stringify them. Third, one pass: read `item[key]`, get or create the bucket, push, and return `[...map]`. Mention the cost (O(n) time, one array per distinct key) and that ES2024 adds a built-in `Map.groupBy`, which returns a `Map` with exactly these semantics.

extraPractice.title: Typed pick
extraPractice.prompt: Write `pick(obj, keys)` that returns a new object with only the listed keys copied from `obj`. Type it as `<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, keys: readonly K[]): Pick<T, K>` so the result type has exactly the picked properties. Keys the object does not actually own are skipped, repeated keys are harmless, and the copy is shallow.
hints: Start from an empty result typed `Pick<T, K>` and copy `obj[key]` for each key; `out[key] = obj[key]` type-checks because both sides are `T[K]`.
Use `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` to skip keys the object does not own, including inherited ones such as `toString`.
checklist: Only listed keys appear in the result, and an empty key list gives `{}`.
A property whose value is `null` is still copied.
Nested objects are shared, not cloned, and the input object is not modified.

extraPractice.title: Merge defaults deeply
extraPractice.prompt: Write `mergeDefaults(defaults, overrides)`. Return a new object that starts from `defaults` and applies `overrides`: when both sides hold a plain object, merge recursively; otherwise the override value wins (arrays and `null` replace, they are not merged). Do not mutate either input. Type `overrides` as a deep partial of the defaults' type so callers can pass any nested subset.
hints: Define `type DeepPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] extends object ? DeepPartial<T[K]> : T[K] }` (a preview of mapped and conditional types), keeping arrays whole.
Do the recursion on `Record<string, unknown>` with an `isPlainObject` type guard, and cast to `T` only once at the public boundary.
checklist: Nested objects merge key by key; arrays and `null` replace the default.
Neither input is mutated: every merged level is a fresh object.
An empty overrides object returns a copy equal to the defaults.

followUps.question: What is the difference between `<T extends object>` and a parameter typed `object`?
followUps.answer: Both accept only non-primitive values, but the generic remembers which object the caller passed. With `(x: object): object` the caller gets back `object` and loses every property; with `<T extends object>(x: T): T` they get their own type back. Use the constraint when the output type depends on the input; use the plain type when it does not.

followUps.question: Why does `Omit<User, 'pasword'>` compile, and how would you make it strict?
followUps.answer: `Omit` is declared as `Omit<T, K extends keyof any>`, so `K` may be any string, not just keys of `T`; a typo removes nothing. A strict variant is `type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>`, which makes the typo a compile error. `Pick` is already strict because its `K extends keyof T`.

followUps.question: When would you choose `satisfies` over a type annotation, and when not?
followUps.answer: Use `satisfies` when the value's precise inferred type is useful: config tables, route maps, handler registries, where you want literal keys and per-entry value types kept while still checking the shape. Use an annotation when you want the wider type on purpose, such as a variable that will be reassigned or a public export whose type should not change when the literal changes.

followUps.question: A teammate writes `function get<T>(url: string): Promise<T>` around `fetch`. What do you say?
followUps.answer: The `T` appears only in the return type, so it is an unchecked assertion in disguise: callers pick any `T` and nothing verifies the JSON. Return `Promise<unknown>` and validate with a type guard or a schema library at the boundary, or accept a validator parameter `(data: unknown) => data is T`, which makes `T` appear twice and actually checked.

takeaways: A type parameter relates types: it should appear at least twice, and callers rarely need to write it because it is inferred.
`K extends keyof T` plus `T[K]` types property access exactly and turns key typos into compile errors.
Utility types derive shapes from one source of truth; they are compile-time only, and `Omit` does not check its keys.
`satisfies` checks a value without widening it; an annotation replaces the inferred type.
Types are erased, so `as T` and `any` check nothing at runtime; validate `unknown` at the boundary.

diagrams.title: How pluck(users, 'age') infers T and K
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram of generic inference. The call site pluck(users, 'age') sends its first argument, users of type User[], to infer T = User, and its second argument, the literal 'age', to infer K = 'age'. K is checked against keyof User, which contains id, name and age, and the return type T[K][] resolves to number[].
diagrams.caption: Each type parameter is inferred from the argument it appears in, checked against its constraint, then substituted into the return type.

steps.text: The compiler lines up each argument with the parameter type that mentions a type parameter.
`users` is `User[]` and the parameter is `T[]`, so `T = User`.
`'age'` is a string literal and the parameter is `K`, so `K = 'age'`, not `string`.
The constraint is checked: `'age'` must be one of `keyof User`. A typo such as `'agee'` fails here.

diagrams.title: A string key versus K extends keyof T
diagrams.alt: Comparison of two signatures for reading a property. On the left, the key is typed string: a typo like 'agee' compiles, and the body needs an any cast so the result is any. On the right, the key is K extends keyof T: the typo is a compile error and a valid key returns T[K], here number.
diagrams.caption: Constraining the key to keyof T moves typo detection to compile time and returns the exact property type.

diagrams.title: Deriving types from one User type
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram with a User type holding id, name, email and password in the middle left. Pick of id and name produces PublicUser for API responses. Omit of id produces NewUser for a create form. Partial produces a patch type for an update call. Readonly produces a frozen view. All four are derived from the single source type.
diagrams.caption: Derive every variant from one source type so a new field is never forgotten; the utilities shape types, not objects.

steps.text: `Pick` keeps only the listed keys: the public shape the API returns.
`Omit` removes keys: the create form does not send an id. Its key list is not checked, so spell carefully.
`Partial` makes every property optional: a patch can carry any subset.
`Readonly` blocks assignment in the type checker only; the runtime object is still writable unless you `Object.freeze` it.

diagrams.title: Annotation versus satisfies for a route table
diagrams.alt: Comparison of a route table typed two ways. On the left, an annotation with Record<string, string> widens the keys to string, so the typo routes.hmoe compiles and is undefined at runtime. On the right, satisfies Record<string, string> checks the shape but keeps the keys home and about, so routes.hmoe is a compile error.
diagrams.caption: An annotation replaces the inferred type; satisfies checks against it and keeps the precise type.

diagrams.title: What happens to parse<number> at runtime
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram with your code, the type checker, the emitted JavaScript and the runtime. The checker accepts parse<number>('"42"') and types the result as number because of the as T assertion. Emission deletes the type argument and the assertion. At runtime JSON.parse returns the string 42, so typeof n is 'string'.
diagrams.caption: Type arguments and assertions vanish on emit; only runtime checks can make a generic result trustworthy.

messages.label: n: number
messages.note: `as T` tells the checker to trust the caller's choice of T.

messages.label: erase <number> and as T
messages.note: Type arguments, annotations and assertions leave no code behind.

messages.label: 'string'
messages.note: The static type said number; nothing ever checked it.

predict.explain: `<number>` and `as T` are erased on emit. `JSON.parse` returns the string `'42'`, and nothing ever checks it against the static type.
`Omit` only changes the type. `safe` is the same object as `user`, so the password is still serialised. Copy the fields you want (or destructure out the secret) to actually remove it.
`Readonly` is a compile-time view of the same object. The assertion gives a writable view, the assignment succeeds at runtime, and both names see 3. Only `Object.freeze` blocks writes at runtime.

Object keys are strings, and integer-like keys (array indices) are listed first in ascending order; `'-1'` is not an array index, so it keeps insertion order after them. `Record<number, ...>` does not change that.
A `Map` compares keys with SameValueZero, so the number `1` and the string `'1'` are different keys. A plain object would have merged them into one string key.

lab.tip: Write the signature first and talk through it before any body: "T is inferred from the items, K must be a key of T, and the return uses T[K] so the caller gets the property's real type." Then say one sentence about runtime: types are erased, so anything coming from JSON is `unknown` until a check proves otherwise.
